extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and students of fiction writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling the 'panoramic' (pictorial, retrospective, narrator-present) versus the 'scenic' (dramatic, enacted, narrator-effaced) modes in novels — when to summarize and survey and when to set a scene in immediate action, with notes on pacing, character preparation, and narrator presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic vs scenic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Start from the distinction between the "panoramic" and the "scenic" presentation of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panoramic (pictorial) = broad survey, retrospective reminiscence, long retrospective vision; scenic (dramatic) = placing action before the reader as present drama. Use the label consciously to decide how the reader relates to the author (listening to a storyteller vs watching the story). Examples: Thackeray as panoramic, Dickens/Maupassant inclined to drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the method fit the story's purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The right way for a kind of story (e.g., Vanity Fair) is determined by what the book is meant to create — an impression of a world rather than a single central plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the work's point is an impression of a society, manners, or a time, prefer panoramic treatment; if the work hinges on a decisive question or single conflict, prefer scenic enactment. Choosing wrongly (e.g., dramatizing material that is meant as an impression) will obscure the book's aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity through typical, representative characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity may depend on the fact that all the throng of men and women are strongly, picturesquely typical of the world from which they are taken — all in their different ways can add to the force of its effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For panoramic works, a light link between characters (loose ties) is sufficient; the novel's unity comes from the aggregate impression of typical figures rather than tightly woven intrigue. You can let multiple plots coexist without a central, single plot-thread if characters together create a unified social impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use panoramic/pictorial style to build sweeping impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the story in a continuous flow of leisurely, contemplative reminiscence, with scene melting into scene and backward-ranging thought lingering and brooding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ broad, summary passages, selective glimpses, and summarized sequences to convey the tenor of a place and time; rely on memory-like flashes and pictorial summaries rather than sustained dramatic scenes. Examples: Thackeray's long retrospective vision, roaming to and fro over past events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate individual instances to the broad effect
rubrics_metrics.description: That foreshortening and generalizing, that fusion of detail, that subordination of the instance and the occasion to the broad effect, are the elements of the pictorial art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sketching a panorama, let particular incidents illustrate and reinforce the general tone without themselves becoming foregrounded set-pieces. Use hints, moments, and brief glimpses rather than fully dramatized episodes unless the story requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve scenic/dramatic method for decisive climaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the final and decisive scene is required, it must be placed immediately before us — it must be enacted in full view to have its proper emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switch from narrator-led summary to direct, present enactment for moments that answer the central question or determine characters' fates (e.g., Becky's collapse). Prepare to 'clear a space' and let characters 'take the matter into their own hands' so the scene can be seen with the necessary warrant and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and stage major scenes in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax must be prepared for; failing to prepare leads to theatrical devices and an unnatural, forced effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a climax will be enacted, render characters and their relations in immediate terms earlier (so they can act credibly). Avoid piling on crude devices at the last moment to force dramatic effect — instead stage and build clarity beforehand so the dramatic scene feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear space for dramatic scenes (avoid authorial haze)
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a scene its free field, the author must clear a space before it and give the situation the free field it cries out for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't smother important scenes with continuous authorial chatter or panoramic haze; temporarily efface or step aside as narrator to let the scene present itself plainly. Excessive 'amusing, irrepressible conversation about the scene' can prevent the scene's facts from being disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use brief illustrative moments sparingly within the panorama
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief incidents and scraps of talk arise by the way and illustrate what the author has to say; a hint, a moment, a glance suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In panoramic narration, let small incidents appear casually and vanish; they should enrich the stream rather than become full dramatic expositions. Reserve fuller dramatization for occasions that require direct evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing characters into an 'unnatural effort' to perform
rubrics_metrics.description: If characters have not been rendered in immediate terms, they must make an unnatural effort to meet the demands of a dramatic scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters have been given sufficient independent life and prior rendering if you expect them to carry a scene without the author's interposition. Otherwise, the scene will feel theatrical or over-actuated relative to the surrounding narrative tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide narrator's presence: personal storyteller vs anonymous dramatist
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a question of the reader's relation to the writer; in one case the reader faces towards the story-teller and listens to him, in the other he turns towards the story and watches it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether the narrator is a visible, opinionated presence (appropriate to panoramic/pictorial method) or whether the author should be effaced so the scene reads like drama (appropriate to Maupassant-like immediacy). Be consistent: panoramic mode naturally keeps the narrator present; drama aims to eliminate the narrator's overt presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey time by leisurely play with chronology and focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Time at Castlewood is not movement; it is tranquillity — time that stands still, deepening as the years go; Thackeray roams to and fro, caring little for connected order if he can give the sensation of time by delaying and returning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create 'time-pictures' or depth of historical atmosphere, manipulate chronology and shift focal distance (near/far) so the place acquires layers of time. This is effective for evoking a sustained mood rather than tracking continuous action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain continuity through pictorial summary where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: For continuity the author recurs to his pictorial summary; as the writer passes into a new circle he makes us feel and know what it was like to live there and belong to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use succinct, evocative summaries and typifying images to move between social milieus and preserve an overall cohesion in panoramic narratives without resorting to tightly plotted connective tissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use piercing, concrete details for highest intensity scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Thackeray has flashes of revelation — a point here and there, a child with a book in a window-seat; the most exquisite is the sight in Esmond of the dusky choir, the shine of the candle-light — a fragment of the past made present and actual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in a broadly panoramic work, deploy sharply observed, concrete images at key moments to produce memorable intensity. These 'fragments' can momentarily convert the retrospective narrator's material into present, actualized experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match treatment (show vs summarize) to the narrative function
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly how the various plots evolve is not the main matter; the method of treatment (showing vs summarizing) should be chosen to serve the work's overall meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the narrative's meaning relies on aggregate impression or time-picture, summarize and generalize; if it relies on individual fate or a decisive answer, show. Be conscious that switching modes is legitimate but must be motivated and prepared for stylistically.
